narrative.h2: Cyberpunk's visual rules are stricter than its fans admit

sections.heading: What cyberpunk looks like
sections.body: Cyberpunk is rain on neon on Asian-script signage, but the deeper rule is light contrast: pitch black shadows holding hot magenta/cyan key lights, with chromatic aberration on every specular highlight. Volumetric haze fills the middle distance so every neon source has a visible cone. Wet pavement doubles every light into a reflection. Skip any of those and you get 'dark sci-fi with purple lights' - adjacent but not the genre.

sections.heading: Where the look comes from
sections.body: The canon: Ridley Scott's Blade Runner (1982) for the original wet-neon Tokyo, Denis Villeneuve's Blade Runner 2049 (2017) for the holographic billboards and orange Vegas, Mamoru Oshii's Ghost in the Shell (1995) for the diving city shots, Katsuhiro Otomo's Akira (1988) for street level, Lana and Lilly Wachowski's The Matrix for the green code wash. Games: CD Projekt Red's Cyberpunk 2077 Night City, the Deus Ex series. Music videos: Grimes' Genesis, M83's Midnight City sequels, Riot Games' Arcane title sequences by Fortiche. Tunee's cyberpunk model is trained on these exact frame languages - 'Blade Runner 2049 Vegas orange haze' lands precisely where you mean.

sections.heading: Prompting tip for Tunee
sections.body: Always pair two neon colors and forbid warm tones: 'magenta and cyan only, no amber'. Add 'wet pavement, neon reflection on ground' - it doubles the perceived light density. Specify 'volumetric haze, visible light cones' or you'll get flat neon. For the artist shot, add 'rim-lit silhouette, key light from above-left' - full-lit faces destroy the noir. End with 'chromatic aberration on highlights' for the lens feel.
